name: Business Requirement
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Starting With Why: What a Business Requirement Actually Is
lesson.summary: A business requirement states what an organization actually needs to achieve, in plain, non-technical language, without naming any particular technology, so that blockchain or any other solution can later be evaluated honestly against it.
lesson.body:
A business requirement is a statement of what an organization actually needs to achieve, expressed in terms of the problem or goal, not in terms of any particular technology used to solve it. Before anyone writes a line of code, chooses a database, or decides whether blockchain technology belongs anywhere near a project, someone has to answer a much simpler question: what outcome does the business actually need. A business requirement might read something like reduce the time it takes to verify a supplier's certification from three weeks to three days, or give customers a way to confirm that a product is authentic before they buy it. Notice that neither example mentions a blockchain, a database, or any specific software at all. That is deliberate, and it is the whole point of the category.

Keeping business requirements separate from technical solutions matters because it is easy, especially with a technology that generates as much enthusiasm as blockchain has, to skip straight to the solution and work backward to invent a justification for it. A team excited about blockchain technology might decide to build something with it first and only afterward ask what business problem it solves, which tends to produce systems that are technically impressive but do not actually address anything the organization needed fixed. Starting from a clearly stated business requirement forces the opposite order: define the real-world outcome first, in language a non-technical executive could understand and evaluate, and only then evaluate which technology, blockchain or otherwise, actually serves that outcome best.

A useful business requirement is specific enough to be checked later. Improve trust in our supply chain sounds reasonable but cannot really be verified as done or not done, while let any customer independently verify, without contacting us, that a given product batch passed its safety inspection describes a concrete outcome that a team can build toward and later confirm they achieved. This specificity is what makes a business requirement useful rather than aspirational, and it is also what allows the same requirement to be evaluated against multiple possible solutions rather than just one. A supply chain verification requirement like the one above could potentially be met by a public blockchain, but it could also potentially be met by a conventional database with a public read-only lookup page, and a serious business requirement invites that comparison rather than assuming the answer in advance.

Business requirements are the starting point for everything that follows in evaluating whether blockchain technology fits a given problem, because every other question, what specific features are needed, what a system must technically do, how much it can cost to operate, ultimately traces back to whether it serves the business requirement it was meant to satisfy. The next concept, functional requirement, is where a business requirement gets translated into something concrete enough for engineers to actually build against.
